title: The Grave That Was Double-Guarded Against the Undead
summary:
In 2022, archaeologists unearthed an unsettling grave in Pień, in north-central Poland. The young woman buried there, whom researchers call Zosia, was 17 to 19 years old when she died. A sickle blade was hooked over her throat, and a triangular padlock hung on the big toe of her left foot.

"The placement of the sickle and the padlock suggests that the purpose of these practices was to protect the living from Zosia after her death," says Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, Poland, who led the excavation. That included, "without a doubt, preventing her from rising from the grave." The team's findings appeared in the October issue of Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. Sickles and padlocks have each been found in other European tombs to shield the living from the dead, but Zosia's grave is the first known to use both.

Clues suggest the precautions happened in two stages. The way her leg bones lay hints the padlock was latched on her toe when she was first buried, as if someone suspected she might try to rise right away. Mixed-up soil and the odd angle of her left arm suggest someone later dug the tomb up to place the sickle over her throat. Greenish stains on her skull could have come from a copper object placed in her mouth or nose, possibly another protective measure: in Polish folklore, copper was thought to ward off vampiric demons called strzygi. In this historical context, a "vampire" simply meant a harmful undead being, not the garlic-and-capes monster of today.

Chemical clues paint a picture of Zosia's life. Types of strontium and oxygen atoms in her teeth suggest she grew up near Pień, while her DNA hints her mother's family might have come from Scandinavia. Remnants of a silk cap on her head contained threads of pure silver and gold, suggesting she was a wealthy woman of high social status. That is unusual: people given strange burials were often outsiders or had hard lives, but Zosia seems to have been a local noblewoman. There are no obvious marks of injury or illness on her skeleton, and researchers say they are still examining her DNA for insights into how she died.
why_it_matters: The grave shows how fear and folklore shaped the way past communities treated the dead, and how careful study of bones and buried objects can recover the life story of someone history would otherwise forget.

background_read: Archaeologists study the past by digging up graves, tools, and other remains and reading the clues they leave behind.
In some old European communities, people feared that certain dead people might rise and harm the living.
To prevent this, they sometimes buried the dead with special objects meant to hold the body down or block it from rising.
Clues in bones, teeth, and buried objects can also tell researchers where a person grew up and what kind of life they may have lived.
